claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic FeNiCrMn FCC solid solution.
The simulated initial state is defect-free or contains only minimal thermal vacancies.
Dislocations in FeNiCrMn nucleate primarily from free surfaces or surface steps and kinks rather than from vacancy clusters.
Surface nucleation is driven by local stress concentrations exceeding the CRSS for Shockley-partial emission.
The active defects are 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations that create intrinsic stacking faults.
High surface energy and the absence of pre-existing dislocations make surface nucleation dominant in the MD simulations.
Chemical short-range order and lattice distortion produce high lattice friction in FeNiCrMn and hinder Shockley-partial motion.
Hindered partial-dislocation motion increases the yield stress.
Loading along <11-1> produces a higher maximum yield stress than loading along <110>.
The <11-1> yield stress will be approximately 10–15% higher than the <110> yield stress.
The proposed orientation effect arises from Burgers-vector alignment, Schmid factor, and the Peierls potential for partial dislocations on {111} planes.
The <11-1> orientation requires greater applied stress to initiate a double-kink or surface-nucleation event.
The observed HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults rather than a true HCP phase transformation.
The HCP-like regions are bounded by Shockley partials and lack the long-range order of a true HCP phase.
An intrinsic stacking fault will display an ABCABABC-type local sequence, whereas a true HCP phase will display extended ABABAB stacking.
Yield will appear as a sharp stress drop followed by a plateau or hardening caused by intrinsic-stacking-fault formation.
Yield strength is proportional to shear modulus and inversely proportional to stacking-fault energy.
Thermal activation is limited at strain rates above 10^8 s^-1.
Given sufficiently long simulation time, intrinsic stacking faults could coalesce into a true HCP phase.
Persistence of extended ABAB stacking after unloading and relaxation is proposed as the decisive signature of a true phase transformation rather than a transient stacking fault.

contradictions.description: The orientation rationale is internally inconsistent: <11-1> is described as maximizing resolved shear stress, which ordinarily makes a fixed CRSS easier to reach, but the same alignment is also invoked to predict a higher applied yield stress through a larger Peierls or stacking-fault barrier. The hypothesis does not clearly separate these competing effects.
